Stuff that isn't common knowledge, that you just notice from travel. Examples could be about food, etiquette, public toilets, whatever. :)
What's a small cultural detail you noticed on a recent travel?

I learned that just because people live by the sea doesn't guarantee they know how to cook seafood.

I learned this the hard way after not having a good meal anywhere on the east coast of Sri Lanka and in the local islands of the Maldives only finding fish that was grilled to jerky consistency.

In Sri Lanka I got a fish that was still raw 1cm past the surface and another time at another restaurant had prawns that were cooked without removing the poop chute, so they were little fish feces bombs.

But I guess my non-whinging answer for a small interesting detail I learned was not from South Asia, but from Egypt and Jordan and that was business and hustle is, many times, just the requisite before you can enjoy their hospitality. To rephrase, once the business of the encounter is done (let's say you bought a trinket or a scarf or a tour or some tea or whatever) then you and the merchant can relax and shoot the shit, share some tea, and basically become friends. This cannot happen until the business has been sorted, though. In Russia I noticed it was sort of combined where getting drunk with someone was PART of the business and people are suspicious of doing business with someone who won't get drunk with them, like they think you're afraid of letting something slip in your drunken state and revealing your horrible plan to screw them over or something.

What I always find interesting are the different eating habits.

In parts of Asia not everyone orders his food each, but you order a bit of each and everyone takes what he wants and you share everything. As a European that was a strange concept, to not have my own food, but to share everything with others.
That actually reminds me: When I went to Barcelona, tapas (which you share) were much less of a thing than in the States. I don't recall seeing a single "tapas bar" or a tapas-only restaurant.

I don't remember much tapas in Barcelona (though that could be my fuzzy memory of Barcelona in general), but elsewhere in Spain it seemed pretty common to me. It's not really that there are specific tapas bars/restaurants, just that many of the bars give you a little something to eat when you order a beer.
I didn't see one person working out while in Thailand, but I also didn't see one overweight Thai person. It's all about that diet.
There are quite a few young millennials in bangkok that are becoming over weight. I never saw this until recently. It is starting to creep in.

• Croatia: they put ketchup and mayo on pizza. Not a fan!
  • Japan: They love dressing up for stuff. At Tokyo Disney and Disney Sea, we felt out of place because we were the only ones not dressed head to toe in Mickey apparel. The Japanese also love backpacks and bags in general. Everyone carries quite the amount of gear everywhere they go.
  • South East Asians traveling "west": There are signs in westernized hotels in Bangkok and places like AUS that specifically state to not stand on the toilet like they would a squat toilet.

I noticed that in SE it is important to smile when interacting with people. In California you might see people in an elevator or a cashier and not even bat an eye at them. However, I was asked in a few occasions if something was wrong when I didn't smile when talking with someone.

In Colorado, if you pass someone on a hiking trail, it is considered rude not to smile or say hi. People will sneer after they pass and lament the importation of Californians, mostly because they're perceived as rude.
Instead of playgrounds in Rio De Janeiro Brazil they have gyms made out of cement. I saw 7 year old kids sporting 6 packs.

In Zimbabwe it is important ot ask how a Policeman is doing. If you are stopped at a roadblock, going a bit further and enquiring after their family is an indication you know a bit about their culture. This can make a difference to your Police Road Block Eperience.
